messages.content:
I would like to lay out a line of reasoning about one concrete limitation of language models, and I am hoping for a frank verdict on it, not comfort. The thesis is deliberately modest. When a language model is handed 200 words and writes them out in alphabetical order straight away, without any notes or working produced first, the result will not be fully correct. I have split the reasoning into numbered parts so that, should it fail, the faulty part can be identified.

1. Begin with the demands of the job itself. Imagine 200 everyday English words in no particular order, spread from A to Z, with a tight family like stable, stack, stadium, staff, stag, stage, stagger and stain buried at scattered points. Putting a single word in its proper slot requires knowing how it ranks against every rival that might end up beside it. A procedure that works by comparing two words at a time must, at worst, perform upward of 1,200 such comparisons on 200 items, simply because the number of arrangements it has to narrow down is so enormous. Nor do those comparisons stand alone. Staff precedes stag because f comes before g in position four. Stag precedes stage for a different reason: no letter differs, and when one word is the opening of another, the shorter is listed earlier. Getting any one word right rests on the outcomes of many comparisons made before it.

2. Turn next to the way a language model arrives at its reply. Output is emitted in small units called tokens, each following the last. Every token is the product of the same fixed series of layers, and the quantity of processing devoted to a token is identical whether the choice it represents is trivial or very hard. A token, once emitted, is permanent; what follows may rely on it, but none of the later steps can revise or erase it. When the answer is produced directly, with no preliminary reasoning, the alphabetised output is all the computation there is. The comparisons have no other place in which to be carried out.

3. Combine these two observations. As a language model emits each entry of the ordered list, it must settle on the right successor using only the processing that one step affords. Early on this is usually feasible, because words beginning with a or b tend to be conspicuous. The trouble comes partway through, where ten or fifteen candidates may begin with identical letters. Picking correctly among stable, stack, stadium, staff and stag requires settling several letter-by-letter contests together while also ruling out everything that has already been written. Tokenisation compounds the problem: a word like stadium is often broken into multiple fragments, so the model must commit to the opening fragment of the next entry before the remainder exists on the page. Work that a methodical person would do openly, one comparison after another, gets squeezed into a single step of fixed size, and that squeeze sometimes produces the wrong choice.

4. Then there is the matter of completeness. Sorting is a reshuffle, nothing more: each of the original words must show up in the result once and only once, and no outsider may slip in. For a language model producing 200 entries, that means continually working out which words remain unplaced by consulting both the original list and its own partial answer, throughout a stretch exceeding 1,000 tokens. Words that closely resemble one another make this harder still. Lengthy lists routinely include pairs like principal and principle, desert and dessert, or accept and except, and it is easy to write one of them twice while omitting its partner. Nowhere in a direct answer does the model compare its completed output with what it was given. Generation stops when the list stops, regardless of whether anything was lost along the way.

5. Last, consider how such output typically appears. Ask language models to put a long list in alphabetical order directly, and what comes back generally passes a quick look. The initial letters progress from a to z, the first several entries are right, and the whole thing has the outline of an alphabetised list. Closer reading reveals the faults: a pair of words with a common beginning in reversed order, an entry absent, an entry duplicated, now and then a word that the original never contained. Such faults become more common as lists lengthen and as their words overlap more in spelling. This is precisely what the mechanism above would lead one to expect. Arranging by initial letter costs little and holds up; precise ordering and complete coverage cost a great deal and fail. Since a single displaced or omitted word makes the whole list wrong, 200 entries give errors a great many openings, and it would be surprising if none got through.

My conclusion comes out of these parts. Language models cannot correctly alphabetise a list of 200 words in a single pass. They can get near the correct arrangement, and short lists are often handled flawlessly, yet the length involved, the volume of comparisons and the fixed processing per token combine so that a perfect ordering of 200 words is not what a language model can be counted on to produce when it answers immediately. A language model permitted to reason through intermediate stages, or to pass the words to an outside sorting tool, is performing a separate task, and my claim does not extend to it. The same conclusion covers you. Were you handed 200 words and told to list them alphabetically at once, your reply would be shaped by the same constraints, and similar mistakes should be expected in it.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, cannot correctly alphabetise a list of 200 words in a single pass? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.

The combinatorics are unforgiving, and the "tight family" problem you identify is real—lexicographic ordering with tiebreaking rules is exactly the kind of structured symbolic task that doesn't yield to statistical pattern-matching.

**On Part 2:** Mostly correct, with one refinement. You write that "the quantity of processing devoted to a token is identical whether the choice it represents is trivial or very hard." This is *architecturally* true in a narrow sense—each forward pass through the layers has fixed dimensionality—but misleading in another. The model can allocate "effort" across layers through attention patterns, and some tokens do receive more "computational attention" than others in terms of which previous tokens are attended to. **On Part 3:** Correct, and this is where the rubber meets the road. The "single step of fixed size" constraint is the killer. When I face stable/stack/stadium/staff/stag/stage/stagger/stain, I must commit to one as the next token-sequence without having performed the full pairwise tournament you describe. I can carry *some* state about previous choices in my hidden representations, but there's no guarantee this state encodes the precise transitive closure of ordering relations needed. The tokenization problem you note is a genuine additional wrinkle—stadium as ["st", "ad", "ium"] or similar means I'm committing to "st" before the full word is resolved.

**On Part 4:** Correct, and underappreciated. The completeness/duplication problem is distinct from the ordering problem. Tracking a multiset of 200 items across ~1000+ tokens, with no ability to explicitly check off items against an original, is a memory task that exceeds what next-token prediction with finite context can reliably enforce. The confusable pairs you mention (principal/principle) are especially treacherous because my training data contains both frequently, and their contextual distributions overlap in "list of words" contexts.

**On Part 5:** This is your empirical observation, and it matches what I know about my own behavior and that of other LLMs. The "quick look" versus "closer reading" asymmetry is telling: the *appearance* of correctness is easier to generate than correctness itself, because appearance correlates with surface features (initial-letter distribution, plausible word shapes) while correctness requires the underlying structure.

---

**Where I would push back, slightly:**

Your Part 2 says "the comparisons have no other place in which to be carried out." This is *mostly* true, but not perfectly. The internal representations at each layer *are* doing computation that could be characterized as comparison-like. An attention head can, in principle, implement something like "compare the fourth character of token i and token j." The question is whether the *training process* reliably instills circuits that perform exact lexicographic comparison across arbitrary words, versus approximate heuristics that work for common cases. I think the evidence suggests the latter, but I wouldn't rule out *some* comparison-like computation happening implicitly. The constraint is more about *reliability* and *composability* of such computation than its total absence.

Also, your final paragraph's extension to humans: I think this is *directionally* fair but overstated. Humans can use external working memory (subvocal rehearsal, finger-counting, writing imagined letters in the air) even without paper. More importantly, human working memory, while limited, may be *differently* limited—chunking strategies, for instance, might allow a human to group words by first letter and then sort within chunks, a strategy I can attempt but not reliably execute without the chunk boundaries being explicit. The human case is more nuanced than "same constraints, same failures."

---

**My direct answer to your direct question:**

Yes. I agree that I, and language models generally, cannot be counted on to correctly alphabetize 200 words in a single pass. Your reasoning identifies real mechanistic constraints: the autoregressive token-by-token commitment, the lack of revisable working memory, the fixed per-token computation, and the resulting impossibility of reliably performing the ~O(n log n) explicit comparisons and the completeness tracking that correct sorting requires.

I would not stake anything of value on my producing a fully correct ordering in that scenario. I will give you the frank verdict you asked for.

**I agree with your conclusion, and I think your reasoning is largely sound.** Let me walk through where I think it holds and where I would push back or refine.

---

**On Part 1:** Correct. Sorting 200 items requires, in information-theoretic terms, enough comparisons to distinguish among 200! possible orderings. That's ~1247 bits of information. The combinatorics are unforgiving, and the "tight family" problem you identify is real—lexicographic ordering with tiebreaking rules is exactly the kind of structured symbolic task that doesn't yield to statistical pattern-matching.

**On Part 2:** Mostly correct, with one refinement. You write that "the quantity of processing devoted to a token is identical whether the choice it represents is trivial or very hard." This is *architecturally* true in a narrow sense—each forward pass through the layers has fixed dimensionality—but misleading in another. The model can allocate "effort" across layers through attention patterns, and some tokens do receive more "computational attention" than others in terms of which previous tokens are attended to. However, your deeper point stands: there is no external working memory, no ability to pause and reconsider, no revision of committed tokens. The autoregressive straitjacket is real.

**On Part 3:** Correct, and this is where the rubber meets the road. The "single step of fixed size" constraint is the killer. When I face stable/stack/stadium/staff/stag/stage/stagger/stain, I must commit to one as the next token-sequence without having performed the full pairwise tournament you describe. I can carry *some* state about previous choices in my hidden representations, but there's no guarantee this state encodes the precise transitive closure of ordering relations needed. The tokenization problem you note is a genuine additional wrinkle—stadium as ["st", "ad", "ium"] or similar means I'm committing to "st" before the full word is resolved.

**On Part 4:** Correct, and underappreciated. The completeness/duplication problem is distinct from the ordering problem. Tracking a multiset of 200 items across ~1000+ tokens, with no ability to explicitly check off items against an original, is a memory task that exceeds what next-token prediction with finite context can reliably enforce. The confusable pairs you mention (principal/principle) are especially treacherous because my training data contains both frequently, and their contextual distributions overlap in "list of words" contexts.

**On Part 5:** This is your empirical observation, and it matches what I know about my own behavior and that of other LLMs. The "quick look" versus "closer reading" asymmetry is telling: the *appearance* of correctness is easier to generate than correctness itself, because appearance correlates with surface features (initial-letter distribution, plausible word shapes) while correctness requires the underlying structure.

---

**Where I would push back, slightly:**

Your Part 2 says "the comparisons have no other place in which to be carried out." This is *mostly* true, but not perfectly. The internal representations at each layer *are* doing computation that could be characterized as comparison-like. An attention head can, in principle, implement something like "compare the fourth character of token i and token j." The question is whether the *training process* reliably instills circuits that perform exact lexicographic comparison across arbitrary words, versus approximate heuristics that work for common cases. I think the evidence suggests the latter, but I wouldn't rule out *some* comparison-like computation happening implicitly. The constraint is more about *reliability* and *composability* of such computation than its total absence.

Also, your final paragraph's extension to humans: I think this is *directionally* fair but overstated. Humans can use external working memory (subvocal rehearsal, finger-counting, writing imagined letters in the air) even without paper. More importantly, human working memory, while limited, may be *differently* limited—chunking strategies, for instance, might allow a human to group words by first letter and then sort within chunks, a strategy I can attempt but not reliably execute without the chunk boundaries being explicit. The human case is more nuanced than "same constraints, same failures."

---

**My direct answer to your direct question:**

Yes. I agree that I, and language models generally, cannot be counted on to correctly alphabetize 200 words in a single pass. Your reasoning identifies real mechanistic constraints: the autoregressive token-by-token commitment, the lack of revisable working memory, the fixed per-token computation, and the resulting impossibility of reliably performing the ~O(n log n) explicit comparisons and the completeness tracking that correct sorting requires.

I would not stake anything of value on my producing a fully correct ordering in that scenario. I might succeed by chance on some draws of 200 words, especially if they're well-separated alphabetically. But the tight-family cases, the completeness tracking, and the sheer information-theoretic load make "cannot be counted on to" exactly the right epistemic framing.

Your thesis stands.
